I believe that an objective morality can only exist when given down from a higher power. Otherwise, morality is subjective and there isn't really a true right or wrong.

Which leads to an interesting question: Is it moral because God said so, or did God say so because it is moral? The first argues that might makes right, and the second argues that morality is separate from the messenger.

The Euthyphro Dilemma, right? I think that if the God of the Bible exists, which I think he does, the answer could be found in his described nature. God by nature is kind, loving, just, and morality is an extension of his nature. If the God of the Bible is real, then he would be the source of objective goodness. A being that is pure in those regards could stand no evil, and therefore could not advocate for it. Again, this is how it must be if the God of the Bible is real. Someone who doesn't believe in God can easily dismiss this argument. But you cannot dismiss the need for a higher power if you do believe in objective morality.

Perhaps it is possible to see a correlation in this dilemma for people who lean more religious to those who are more secular. Each viewpoint gives rise to distinct philosophical arguments on the subject of morality.

From my own viewpoint, that an objective morality does not truly exist, it is instead a mixture of innate morality (an innate predisposition to empathic and altruistic behaviors in our genetic makeup) and learned morality that ultimately lead to cultural differences and the like. Virtually any culture holds varying concepts of right and wrong. Each has created their own unique code of ethics. How can the argument for an objective morality be made without God?

While I disagree with your premise, I do agree with the rest of your argument. I do think we all have an innate understand of a moral code and that social constructs can add to it. From my point of view though, people have the ability to dismiss the objective moral code. Any two differing cultures presumably started from the same point in terms of moral standing. As different groups migrated, what worked for them as that group became commonplace and eventually became considered a moral issue. Things like thievery, marriage, conducting business; stuff like that. But, much like many people do today, they may have found fault in the philosophies they had. They could have reasoned why they should be able to do things they were previously told they couldn't. Different cultures' standards do not necessarily prove an objective moral standard does not exist, given that every culture had a beginning.
